Artillery refers to large, heavy, powerful weapons — such as cannons, howitzers, and rocket launchers — that fire explosive projectiles (shells or rockets) over long distances. These weapons are far too big and heavy to be carried and operated by a single soldier. They require a crew — typically a team of several soldiers — to move, set up, aim, and fire.

If a rifle or pistol is a tool one person holds in their hands, artillery is the opposite end of the scale: a massive machine that one person cannot even lift, let alone use alone.

Three qualities define artillery:

1. Size and weight. Artillery pieces are enormous. They are often mounted on wheeled carriages, trucks, or armored platforms. A single artillery piece can weigh several tons.

2. Long range. Artillery is specifically designed to strike targets that are far away — sometimes many miles — and completely out of direct sight of the soldiers firing it. You cannot see what you are shooting at. You calculate where the target is and fire at it indirectly.

3. Explosive projectiles. Artillery fires large shells or rockets that explode on impact, causing destruction over a wide area — not just a small point, like a bullet.

The word "artillery" is an umbrella term. It covers several types of large weapons:

  • Cannons — the classic, oldest form. A long metal tube that fires a heavy shell forward using an explosive charge. Think of old warships or medieval siege battles.
  • Howitzers — a modern and very common type. Fires shells at high angles so they arc through the air and come down on targets that may be hidden behind hills or walls.
  • Mortars — shorter and wider tubes that launch shells steeply upward so they fall almost straight down. Useful at shorter ranges.
  • Rocket artillery — systems that launch multiple rockets rapidly. Examples include the famous Soviet "Katyusha" of World War II, or modern systems like the MLRS (Multiple Launch Rocket System).
  • Siege guns — historically, massive guns used specifically to demolish castle walls, city gates, and fortifications.
How Artillery Is Used in War

Artillery serves several vital purposes on a battlefield:

  • Bombardment: Firing shells at enemy soldiers, vehicles, supply depots, or buildings from a safe distance to destroy or weaken them.
  • Supporting infantry: When soldiers on the ground advance toward the enemy, artillery fires ahead of them, clearing the path by destroying enemy positions before the foot soldiers arrive.
  • Suppression: Even if shells don't destroy the enemy outright, the constant threat of explosion forces the enemy to hide and stop fighting — which is itself a tactical advantage.
  • Destroying fortifications: Thick walls, bunkers, and reinforced buildings that small arms cannot damage can be broken apart by artillery shells.

Beyond the weapons themselves, "artillery" also refers to the branch of an army responsible for operating these weapons — the soldiers, the unit, the division.

Just as "infantry" refers to soldiers who fight on foot, "artillery" refers to the military branch that fights with big guns. So when someone says "He served in the artillery," they mean he was part of the unit that operated large guns and cannons — not that he carried one on his back.
How Artillery Differs from Other Weapons

It helps to understand this by contrast:

  • Small arms (rifles, pistols, submachine guns): Carried and fired by one person. Fire bullets. Used at close-to-medium range.
  • Artillery: Operated by a crew of several people. Fire explosive shells or rockets. Used at long range, often against targets out of direct view.

The line between them isn't always perfectly sharp — mortars, for example, can be relatively light — but the key idea is: if a single soldier can carry it and fire it alone, it is generally not artillery.

In non-military, everyday English, "artillery" (most often as "heavy artillery") is sometimes used figuratively to mean your most powerful, most impressive resources, people, or arguments — the big guns you bring out when you really need to win something.

  • "The company brought in the heavy artillery — their best lawyers and top executives — to handle the lawsuit."
  • "When normal arguments didn't work, she pulled out her heavy artillery."

This usage borrows the military image of artillery being the most destructive, powerful force available. It implies seriousness, weight, and a decisive escalation.

• "The army positioned its artillery on the hilltops before the attack began."
  • "The thunder of artillery could be heard from twenty miles away."
  • "His grandfather served in the artillery division during World War II."
  • "The city fell after three days of relentless artillery bombardment."
  • "In the debate, she saved her heavy artillery for the closing argument."

Artillery is the collective term for large, crew-operated weapons — cannons, howitzers, rocket launchers, and the like — that fire explosive shells or rockets over long distances, and also refers to the military branch that uses them; figuratively, it means the most powerful means or people at your disposal.
